module_title: Periodic Table and Classification of Elements (Detailed Foundational)
introduction: This foundational level establishes the architecture of the Modern Periodic Table. It covers the transition from Mendeleev's atomic mass-based system to Moseley's atomic number-based system, the IUPAC nomenclature for heavy elements, and the classification of elements into s, p, d, and f blocks based on their electronic configurations.

core_concepts.title: Mendeleev's vs. Modern Periodic Law
core_concepts.description: Mendeleev's Periodic Law stated that the physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their Atomic Weights. However, Henry Moseley's X-ray diffraction experiments proved that Atomic Number ($Z$) is a more fundamental property. The Modern Periodic Law states: 'The physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their Atomic Numbers.' This resolved anomalies like the positions of Isotopes and Ar/K, Co/Ni inverted mass pairs.

core_concepts.title: Structure of the Modern Periodic Table
core_concepts.description: The table consists of 18 vertical columns called Groups and 7 horizontal rows called Periods. The period number corresponds to the highest principal quantum number ($n$) of the valence shell. The group number indicates the number of valence electrons and the specific chemical family (e.g., Group 1 = Alkali Metals, Group 17 = Halogens, Group 18 = Noble Gases).

core_concepts.title: Block Classification (s, p, d, f)
core_concepts.description:
Elements are classified based on the subshell into which the last (differentiating) electron enters.
1. s-block: Groups 1 and 2. General configuration $ns^{1-2}$. Highly reactive metals.
2. p-block: Groups 13 to 18. General configuration $ns^2 np^{1-6}$. Contains metals, non-metals, and metalloids.
3. d-block (Transition Elements): Groups 3 to 12. General configuration $(n-1)d^{1-10} ns^{1-2}$. Known for variable oxidation states and colored ions.
4. f-block (Inner Transition Elements): Lanthanoids ($4f$) and Actinoids ($5f$). General configuration $(n-2)f^{1-14} (n-1)d^{0-1} ns^2$.

core_concepts.title: IUPAC Nomenclature for Elements with $Z > 100$
core_concepts.description: To avoid naming controversies, IUPAC established a systematic naming convention using numerical roots: 0=nil, 1=un, 2=bi, 3=tri, 4=quad, 5=pent, 6=hex, 7=sept, 8=oct, 9=enn. The suffix '-ium' is added at the end. Example: Element 104 is un-nil-quad-ium (Unnilquadium, Symbol: Unq).

important_entities.name: Magic Numbers
important_entities.significance: These numbers represent the difference in atomic numbers of consecutive elements within a group. By memorizing the atomic number of the first element in a group, you can find the atomic numbers of all subsequent elements by successively adding these magic numbers.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Helium (He) has the electronic configuration $1s^2$. Based strictly on the subshell receiving the last electron, it should belong to the s-block (Group 2). However, because its valence shell is completely full, it exhibits extreme chemical inertness and is therefore placed with the Noble Gases in Group 18 (p-block) based on its CHEMICAL properties, not its electronic block.

mnemonics_and_tricks.trick_title: Finding Group Number from Atomic Number ($Z$)
mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Difference from the next Noble Gas
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: To quickly find the group of an element (e.g., $Z=42$): Identify the next noble gas ($Z=54$, Xenon, Group 18). Subtract the atomic number from the noble gas: $54 - 42 = 12$. Now subtract this difference from 18: $18 - 12 = 6$. So, Element 42 belongs to Group 6 (Molybdenum).

exam_strategy_tips: NEET and JEE frequently ask for the atomic number of the element placed exactly below another element. Do not write out the full electronic configuration. Just use the magic numbers. For example, below Phosphorus ($Z=15$, period 3) is Arsenic: $15 + 18 = 33$.
